title: Higher wages, lower costs?

readouts.l: Labour cost per unit = wage ÷ output per worker

predict.q: Each worker is paid **£100** a day and makes **20** units a day. Wages rise to **£120** a day. New machines raise output to **30** units per worker a day. What happens to the **labour cost of each unit**?

options.s: It rises, because wages went up
options.fb: Wages rose 20%, but output per worker rose 50%. Each unit now carries less labour cost: £120 ÷ 30 = £4.
£100 ÷ 20 = £5 per unit before; £120 ÷ 30 = £4 per unit after.
It would stay the same only if wages and output per worker rose by the same %.

options.s: You cannot tell without the price
options.fb: Labour cost per unit needs only the wage and output per worker. The price affects profit, not cost.

task: Move the **wage** and **output per worker** sliders and watch labour cost per unit.

target.do: Set the wage to £120 and output per worker to 30, then press Check.

takeaway: Labour cost per unit = wage ÷ output per worker. If productivity rises faster than wages, cost per unit **falls**.
